entries.8e0fd9261b16b27320ad105220efb0ab28633485: <div sID="gen13292" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="149" osisID="Ps.149" sID="Ps.149"/> <div eID="gen13292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13293" type="x-p"/> The foregoing psalm was a hymn of praise to the Creator; this is a hymn of praise to the Redeemer. It is a psalm of triumph in the God of Israel, and over the enemies of Israel. Probably it was penned upon occasion of some victory which Israel was blessed and honoured with. Some conjecture that it was penned when David had taken the strong-hold of Zion, and settled his government there. But it looks further, to the kingdom of the Messiah, who, in the chariot of the everlasting gospel, goes forth conquering and to conquer. To him, and his graces and glories, we must have an eye, in singing this psalm, which proclaims, I. Abundance of joy to all the people of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.149.1-Ps.149.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. Abundance of terror to the proudest of their enemies, <reference osisRef="Ps.149.6-Ps.149.9">ver. 6-9</reference>.
entries.f431a1b318a86b54a2c65cdefe58e42aea8fecec: <div eID="gen13293" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Saints Admonished to Praise God.</title> <div sID="gen13294" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Praise ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . Sing unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> a new song, <hi type="italic">and</hi> his praise in the congregation of saints. <hi type="super">2</hi> Let Israel rejoice in him that made him: let the children of Zion be joyful in their King. <hi type="super">3</hi> Let them praise his name in the dance: let them sing praises unto him with the timbrel and harp. <hi type="super">4</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> taketh pleasure in his people: he will beautify the meek with salvation. <hi type="super">5</hi> Let the saints be joyful in glory: let them sing aloud upon their beds. <div eID="gen13294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13295" type="x-p"/> We have here, <div eID="gen13295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13296" type="x-p"/> I. The calls given to God's Israel to praise. <hi type="italic">All his works</hi> were, in the foregoing psalm, excited to <hi type="italic">praise him;</hi> but here his saints in a particular manner are required to bless him. Observe then, 1. Who are called upon to praise God. <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> in general, the body of the church (<reference osisRef="Ps.149.2">v. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">the children of Zion</hi> particularly, the inhabitants of that holy hill, who are nearer to God than other Israelites; those that have the word and ordinances of God near to them, that are not required to travel far to them, are justly expected to do more in praising God than others. All true Christians may call themselves <hi type="italic">the children of Zion,</hi> for in faith and hope <hi type="italic">we have come unto Mount Zion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">Heb. xii. 22</reference>. The saints must praise God, saints in profession, saints in power, for this is the intention of their sanctification; they are devoted to the glory of God, and renewed by the grace of God, that <hi type="italic">they may be unto him for a name and a praise.</hi> 2. What must be the principle of this praise, and that is holy joy in God: <hi type="italic">Let Israel rejoice,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the children of Zion be joyful,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the saints be joyful in glory.</hi> Our praises of God should flow from a heart filled with delight and triumph in God's attributes, and our relation to him. Much of the power of godliness in the heart consists in making God our chief joy and solacing ourselves in him; and our faith in Christ is described by our rejoicing in him. We then give honour to God when we take pleasure in him. We must <hi type="italic">be joyful in glory,</hi> that is, in him as our glory, and in the interest we have in him; and let us look upon it as our glory to be of those that rejoice in God. 3. What must be the expressions of this praise. We must by all proper ways show forth the praises of God: <hi type="italic">Sing to the Lord.</hi> We must entertain ourselves, and proclaim his name, by <hi type="italic">singing praises to him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.149.3">v. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">singing aloud</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.149.5">v. 5</reference>), for we should sing psalms with all our heart, as those that are not only not ashamed of it, but are enlarged in it. We must sing a <hi type="italic">new song,</hi> newly composed upon every special occasion, sing with new affections, which make the song new, though the words have been used before, and keep them from growing threadbare. Let God be <hi type="italic">praised in the dance with timbrel and harp,</hi> according to the usage of the Old-Testament church very early (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.20">Exod. xv. 20</reference>), where we find God praised with <hi type="italic">timbrels and dances.</hi> Those who from this urge the use of music in religious worship must by the same rule introduce dancing, for they went together, as in David's dancing before the ark, and <reference osisRef="Judg.21.21">Judg. xxi. 21</reference>. But, whereas many scriptures in the New Testament keep up singing as a gospel-ordinance, none provide for the keeping up of music and dancing; the gospel-canon for psalmody is to <hi type="italic">sing with the spirit</hi> and <hi type="italic">with the understanding.</hi> 4. What opportunities must be taken for praising God, none must be let slip, but particularly, (1.) We must praise God in public, in the <hi type="italic">solemn assembly</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.149.1">v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">in the congregation of saints.</hi> The more the better; it is the more like heaven. Thus God's name must be owned before the world; thus the service must have a solemnity put upon it, and we must mutually excite one another to it. The principle, end, and design of our coming together in religious assemblies is that we may join together in praising God. Other parts of the service must be in order to this. (2.) We must praise him in private. <hi type="italic">Let the saints</hi> be so transported with their joy in God as to <hi type="italic">sing aloud upon their beds,</hi> when they awake in the night, full of the praises of God, as David, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.62">Ps. cxix. 62</reference>. When God's Israel are brought to a quiet settlement, let them enjoy that, with thankfulness to God; much more may true believers, that have entered into God's rest, and find repose in Jesus Christ, sing aloud for joy of that. Upon their sick-beds, their death-beds, let them sing the praises of their God. <div eID="gen13296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13297" type="x-p"/> II. The cause given to God's Israel for praise. Consider, 1. God's doings for them. They have reason to rejoice in God, to devote themselves to his honour and employ themselves in his service; for it is he that made them. He gave us our being as men, and we have reason to praise him for that, for it is a noble and excellent being. He gave Israel their being as a people, as a church, made them what they were, so very different from other nations. Let that people therefore praise him, for he formed them for himself, on purpose that they might <hi type="italic">show forth his praise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.43.21">Isa. xliii. 21</reference>. Let Israel <hi type="italic">rejoice in his Makers</hi> (so it is in the original); for God said, <hi type="italic">Let us make man;</hi> and in this, some think, is the mystery of the Trinity. 2. God's dominion over them. This follows upon the former: if he made them, he is their King; he that gave being no doubt may give law; and this ought to be the matter of our joy and praise that we are under the conduct and protection of such a wise and powerful King. <hi type="italic">Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! for behold thy king comes,</hi> the king Messiah, whom God has <hi type="italic">set upon his holy hill of Zion;</hi> let all the children of Zion <hi type="italic">be joyful</hi> in him, and go forth to meet him with their hosannas, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zech. ix. 9</reference>. 3. God's delight in them. He is a king that rules by love, and therefore to be praised; for <hi type="italic">the Lord takes pleasure in his people,</hi> in their services, in their prosperity, in communion with them, and in the communications of his favour to them. He that is infinitely happy in the enjoyment of himself, and to whose felicity no accession can be made, yet graciously condescends to <hi type="italic">take pleasure in his people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.147.11">Ps. cxlvii. 11</reference>. 4. God's designs concerning them. Besides the present complacency he has in them, he has prepared for their future glory: <hi type="italic">He will beautify the meek,</hi> the humble, and lowly, and contrite in heart, that tremble at his word and submit to it, that are patient under their afflictions and <hi type="italic">show all meekness towards all men.</hi> These men vilify and asperse, but God will justify them, and wipe off their reproach; nay, he will beautify them; they shall appear not only clear, but comely, before all the world, with the comeliness that he puts upon them. He will beautify them with salvation, with temporal salvations (when God works remarkable deliverances for his people those that had <hi type="italic">been among the pots become as the wings of a dove covered with silver,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.13">Ps. lxviii. 13</reference>), but especially with eternal salvation. The righteous shall be beautified in that day when they <hi type="italic">shine forth as the sun.</hi> In the hopes of this, let them now, in the darkest day, <hi type="italic">sing a new song.</hi>
entries.8e53763139634ce4e426a9c1a9a7b530c6f90254: <div eID="gen13297" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Israel Admonished to Praise God.</title> <div sID="gen13298" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> <hi type="italic">Let</hi> the high <hi type="italic">praises</hi> of God <hi type="italic">be</hi> in their mouth, and a twoedged sword in their hand; 7 To execute vengeance upon the heathen, <hi type="italic">and</hi> punishments upon the people; <hi type="super">8</hi> To bind their kings with chains, and their nobles with fetters of iron; <hi type="super">9</hi> To execute upon them the judgment written: this honour have all his saints. Praise ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen13298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13299" type="x-p"/> The Israel of God are here represented triumphing over their enemies, which is both the matter of their praise (let them give to God the glory of those triumphs) and the recompence of their praise; those that are truly thankful to God for their tranquillity shall be blessed with victory. Or it may be taken as a further expression of their praise (<reference osisRef="Ps.149.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">let the high praises of God be in their mouth,</hi> and then, in a holy zeal for his honour, let them take a <hi type="italic">two-edged sword in their hand,</hi> to fight his battles against the enemies of his kingdom. Now this may be applied, 1. To the many victories which God blessed his people Israel with over the nations of Canaan and other nations that were devoted to destruction. These began in Moses and Joshua, who, when they taught Israel <hi type="italic">the high praises of the Lord,</hi> did withal put <hi type="italic">a two-edged sword in their hand;</hi> David did so too, for, as he was the sweet singer of Israel, so he was the captain of their hosts, and taught the children of Judah the use of the bow (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.18">2 Sam. i. 18</reference>), taught their hands to war, as God had taught his. Thus he and they went on victoriously, fighting the Lord's battles, and avenging Israel's quarrels on those that had oppressed them; then they <hi type="italic">executed vengeance upon the heathen</hi> (the Philistines, Moabites, Ammonites, and others, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.1">2 Sam. viii. 1</reference>, &c.) <hi type="italic">and punishments upon the people,</hi> for all the wrong they had done to God's people, <reference osisRef="Ps.149.7">v. 7</reference>. Their kings and nobles were taken prisoners (<reference osisRef="Ps.149.8">v. 8</reference>) and on some of them the judgment written was executed, as by Joshua on the kings of Canaan, by Gideon on the princes of Midian, by Samuel on Agag. The honour of this redounded to all the Israel of God; and to him who put it upon them they return it entirely in their hallelujahs. Jehoshaphat's army had at the same time <hi type="italic">the high praises of God in their mouth and a two-edged sword in their hand,</hi> for they went forth to war singing the praises of God, and then their sword did execution, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.23">2 Chron. xx. 23</reference>. Some apply it to the time of the Maccabees, when the Jews sometimes gained great advantages against their oppressors. And if it seem strange that the meek should, notwithstanding that character, be thus severe, and upon kings and nobles too, here is one word that justifies them in it; it is <hi type="italic">the judgment written.</hi> They do not do it from any personal malice and revenge, or any bloody politics that they govern themselves by, but by commission from God, according to his direction, and in obedience to his command; and Saul lost his kingdom for disobeying a command of this nature. Thus the kings of the earth that shall be employed in the destruction of the New-Testament Babylon will but <hi type="italic">execute the judgment written,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.17.16-Rev.17.17">Rev. xvii. 16, 17</reference>. But, since now no such special commissions can be produced, this will by no means justify the violence either of subjects against their princes or of princes against their subjects, or both against their neighbours, under pretence of religion; for Christ never intended that his gospel should be propagated by fire and sword or his righteousness wrought by the wrath of man. When the high praises of God are in our mouth with them we should have an olive-branch of peace in our hands. 2. To Christ's victories by the power of his gospel and grace over spiritual enemies, in which all believers are more than conquerors. The word of God is the <hi type="italic">two-edged sword</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">Heb. iv. 12</reference>), the <hi type="italic">sword of the Spirit</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.17">Eph. vi. 17</reference>), which it is not enough to have in our armoury, we must have it in our hand also, as our Master had, when he said, <hi type="italic">It is written.</hi> Now, (1.) With this two-edged sword the first preachers of the gospel obtained a glorious victory over the powers of darkness; vengeance was executed upon the gods of the heathen, by the conviction and conversion of those that had been long their worshippers, and by the consternation and confusion of those that would not repent (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.15">Rev. vi. 15</reference>); the strongholds of Satan were cast down (<reference osisRef="2Chr.10.4-2Chr.10.5">2 Chron. x. 4, 5</reference>); great men were made to tremble at the word, as Felix; Satan, the god of this world, was cast out, according to the judgment given against him. <hi type="italic">This</hi> is the honour of all Christians, that their holy religion has been so victorious. (2.) With this two-edged sword believers fight against their own corruptions, and, through the grace of God, subdue and mortify them; the sin that had dominion over them is crucified; self, that once sat king, is bound with chains and brought into subjection to the yoke of Christ; the tempter is foiled and bruised under their feet. <hi type="italic">This honour have all the saints.</hi> (3.) The complete accomplishment of this will be in the judgment of the great day, when <hi type="italic">the Lord</hi> shall come <hi type="italic">with ten thousands of his saints, to execute judgment upon all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.14-Jude.1.15">Jude 14, 15</reference>. Vengeance shall then be <hi type="italic">executed upon the heathen</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.17">Ps. ix. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">and punishments,</hi> everlasting punishments, <hi type="italic">upon the people. Kings and nobles,</hi> that cast away the bands and cords of Christ's government (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.3">Ps. ii. 3</reference>), shall not be able to cast away the chains and fetters of his wrath and justice. Then shall be executed <hi type="italic">the judgment written,</hi> for <hi type="italic">the secrets of men shall be judged according to the gospel. This</hi> honour shall all the saints have, that, as assessors with Christ, they shall <hi type="italic">judge the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.2">1 Cor. vi. 2</reference>. In the prospect of that let them praise the Lord, and continue Christ's faithful servants and soldiers to the end of their lives.  <chapter eID="Ps.149"/> <div eID="gen13299" type="x-p"/>

entries.90144418d8727d5fd6ace66a3cef89f3f0751e27: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7152"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 149</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.149.1-Ps.149.9">Psa 149:1-9</reference>. This Psalm sustains a close connection with the foregoing. The chosen people are exhorted to praise God, in view of past favors, and also future victories over enemies, of which they are impliedly assured.</title> <div sID="gen10968" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7152"/>1. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1">Psa 96:1</reference>). <div eID="gen10968" type="x-p"/>
entries.9082b50ae3ff906f6e7be835b71272b81ce2207c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7153"/><div sID="gen10969" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7153"/>2. God had signalized His relation as a sovereign, in restoring them to their land. <div eID="gen10969" type="x-p"/>
entries.863ef0dee7cc447681adb5303f66a090c45a40a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7154"/><div sID="gen10970" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7154"/><hi type="bold">3. in the dance--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.30.11">Psa 30:11</reference>). The dance is connected with other terms, expressive of the great joy of the occasion. The word may be rendered "lute," to which the other instruments are joined.<div eID="gen10970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10971" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sing praises--</hi>or, sing and play. <div eID="gen10971" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb50ef14d3c69b363496b4bc0803ccd2ab88caa0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7155"/><div sID="gen10972" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7155"/><hi type="bold">4. taketh pleasure--</hi>literally, "accepts," alluding to acceptance of propitiatory offerings (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.147.11">Psa 147:11</reference>).<div eID="gen10972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10973" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beautify, &c.--</hi>adorn the humble with faith, hope, joy, and peace. <div eID="gen10973" type="x-p"/>
entries.a3c4b8c4bfc765ea43cdccdcffda4002fe280324: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7156"/><div sID="gen10974" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7156"/><hi type="bold">5. in glory--</hi>the honorable condition to which they are raised.<div eID="gen10974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10975" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon their beds--</hi>once a place of mourning (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.6">Psa 6:6</reference>). <div eID="gen10975" type="x-p"/>
entries.32c6c88937785f0dcaa254213a57be9cc0408b3b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7157"/><div sID="gen10976" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7157"/><hi type="bold">6. high praises--</hi>or, "deeds." They shall go forth as religious warriors, as once religious laborers (<reference osisRef="Neh.4.17">Ne 4:17</reference>). <div eID="gen10976" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c08c9d499ab4d8b241e034ecfde579bc4f09292: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7158"/><div sID="gen10977" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7158"/>7. The destruction of the incorrigibly wicked attends the propagation of God's truth, so that the military successes of the Jews, after the captivity, typified the triumphs of the Gospel. <div eID="gen10977" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee03f4b4224684448144318546aae29103461d4d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7159"/><div sID="gen10978" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7159"/><hi type="bold">9. the judgment written--</hi>either in God's decrees, or perhaps as in <reference osisRef="Deut.32.41-Deut.32.43">De 32:41-43</reference>.<div eID="gen10978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10979" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this honour--</hi>that is, to be thus employed, will be an honorable service, to be assigned<div eID="gen10979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his saints--</hi>or, godly ones (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.3">Psa 16:3</reference>). <chapter eID="Ps.149"/>

entries.9c9735b079bcd42023cd6779de4c3684a2e04b1d: <div eID="gen23602" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23603" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23604" type="x-p"/> All the congregation are invited to praise God for his mercies, <reference osisRef="Psa.149.1-Psa.149.3">Psa 149:1-3</reference>. Their great privileges, <reference osisRef="Psa.149.4">Psa 149:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.149.5">Psa 149:5</reference>. Their victories, <reference osisRef="Psa.149.6-Psa.149.9">Psa 149:6-9</reference>. <div eID="gen23604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23605" type="x-p"/> This seems to be an epinikion, or song of triumph, after some glorious victory; probably in the time of the Maccabees. It has been also understood as predicting the success of the Gospel in the nations of the earth. According to the Syriac, it concerns the new temple, by which the Christian Church is meant. It has no title in the Hebrew, nor in any of the Versions, and no author's name. <div eID="gen23605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23606" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23607" type="x-p"/> Sing unto the Lord a new song - That is, as we have often had occasion to remark, an excellent song, the best we can possibly pronounce. So the word חדש chadash is often understood; and so the word novus, "new," was often used among the Latin writers: - <div eID="gen23607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23608" type="x-p"/> Pollio amat nostram, quamvis sit rustica, musam. <div eID="gen23608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23609" type="x-p"/> Pollio et ipse facit. <div eID="gen23609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23610" type="x-p"/> Nova Carmina Virg. Ecl. iii., ver. 84. <div eID="gen23610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23611" type="x-p"/> Pollio loves my lines, although rude: <div eID="gen23611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23612" type="x-p"/> Pollio himself makes excellent odes. <div eID="gen23612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23613" type="x-p"/> Tamely and inexpressively translated by Dryden: - "Pollio my rural verse vouchsafes to read. <div eID="gen23613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23614" type="x-p"/> My Pollio writes himself." <div eID="gen23614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23615" type="x-p"/> O what a falling off is here! <div eID="gen23615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23616" type="x-p"/> Servius, in his comment on nova, says, magna, Miranda. Nova means great, admirable. <div eID="gen23616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23617" type="x-p"/> So on novum nectar, Ecl. v., ver. 71, he says, id est, magna dulcedo; "nectar of Excellent flavor." <div eID="gen23617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23618" type="x-p"/> Congregation of saints - The Israelites, who were, by profession and by injunction, a holy people.
entries.1985c2926b4ff27909aa55b377fd602e1b62cc4d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23619" type="x-p"/> In him that made him - Let them remember in their exultations to give all glory to the Lord; for he is the Author of their being and their blessings. And let them know that he is their King also; that they should submit to his authority, and be guided and regulated in their hearts and conduct by his laws.
entries.e3f03abb933f62fc44e6bad8f90955e3abc67159: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23620" type="x-p"/> Let them praise his name in the dance - במחול bemachol, with the pipe, or some kind of wind music, classed here with תף toph, the tabor or drum, and כנור kinnor, the harp." מחול machol," says Parkhurst, "some fistular wind-instrument of music, with holes, as a flute, pipe, or fife, from חל chal, to make a hole or opening." I know no place in the Bible where מחול machol and מחלת machalath mean dance of any kind; they constantly signify some kind of pipe.
entries.d01db8ce4f3368355afce6c289b99ec71fc6691e: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23621" type="x-p"/> The Lord taketh pleasure in his people - The pleasure or good will of God is in his people: he loves them ardently, and will load them with his benefits, while they are humble and thankful; for, <div eID="gen23621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23622" type="x-p"/> He will beautify - יפאר yephaer, he will make fair, the meek, ענוים anavim, the lowly, the humble with salvation, בישועה bishuah; which St. Jerome thus translates, Et exaltabit mansuetos in Jesu, "And he will exalt the meek in Jesus." Whether this rendering be correct or not, there is no other way by which the humble soul can be exalted, but by Jesus, as the redeeming Savior.
entries.4d46f5f399eb112db176328825b2017016e6d96d: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23623" type="x-p"/> Let the saints be joyful in glory - Let them be gloriously joyful: seeing themselves so honored and so successful, let them be joyful. God has put glory or honor upon them; let them give him the thanks due to his name. <div eID="gen23623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23624" type="x-p"/> Sing aloud upon their beds - While they are reclining on their couches. At their festal banquets, let them shout the praises of the Lord. In imitation of this we often have at our public entertainments the following words sung, taken from the Vulgate of <reference osisRef="Psa.115.1">Psa 115:1</reference> : Non Nobis Domine Non Nobis; sed Nomini Tuo da Gloriam! super Misericordia Tua et Veritate Tua. "Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory, for thy mercy and for thy truth's sake." Let them mingle their feasting with Divine songs. This reclining on couches, while they take their food, is still practiced in Asiatic countries.
entries.19b1702119b92ac48d1bdff28b531d079a1007a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23625" type="x-p"/> Let the high praises of God - Let them sing songs the most sublime, with the loudest noise consistent with harmony. <div eID="gen23625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23626" type="x-p"/> And a two-edged sword in their hand - Perhaps there is an allusion here to the manner in which the Jews were obliged to labor in rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem: "Every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon," <reference osisRef="Neh.4.17">Neh 4:17</reference>. <div eID="gen23626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23627" type="x-p"/> The two-edged sword, in Hebrew, is פיפיות pipiyoth, "mouth mouths."
entries.b8cd74b1394619ad4f2fce27122bca97830061c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23628" type="x-p"/> To execute vengeance upon the heathen - This may refer simply to their purpose of defending themselves to the uttermost, should their enemies attack them while building their wall: and they had every reason to believe that God would be with them; and that, if their enemies did attack them, they should be able to inflict the severest punishment upon them. <div eID="gen23628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23629" type="x-p"/> Punishments upon the people - The unfaithful and treacherous Jews; for we find that some, even of their nobles, had joined with Sanballat and Tobiah; (see <reference osisRef="Neh.6.17-Neh.6.19">Neh 6:17-19</reference>): and it appears also that many of them had formed alliances with those heathens, which were contrary to the law; see <reference osisRef="Neh.13.15-Neh.13.29">Neh 13:15-29</reference>.
entries.4643e46e1a58c00f75bed684b49cfb39f28830a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23630" type="x-p"/> To bind their kings with chains, and their nobles with fetters of iron - That is, if these kings, governors of provinces, and chiefs among the people, had attacked them, God would have enabled them to defeat them, take their generals prisoners, and lead them in triumph to Jerusalem. It is certain also that in the times of the Maccabees the Jews had many signal victories over the Samaritans, Philistines, and Moabites; and over Antiochus, king of Syria. See the Books of the Maccabees. To these the psalmist may here refer in a hyperbolical way, not unusual in poetry and in songs of triumph.
entries.732e67790233de6adbf93be830f8619e10be9150: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen23630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23631" type="x-p"/> To execute upon them the judgment written - In <reference osisRef="Deu.7.1">Deu 7:1</reference>, etc., God promises his people complete victory over all their enemies, and over the heathen. God repeatedly promises such victories to his faithful people; and this is, properly speaking, the judgment written, i.e., foretold. <div eID="gen23631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23632" type="x-p"/> This honor have all his saints - They shall all be supported, defended, and saved by the Lord. Israel had this honor, and such victories over their enemies, while they continued faithful to their God. When they relapsed into iniquity, their enemies prevailed against them; they were defeated, their city taken, their temple burnt to the ground, more than a million of themselves slaughtered, and the rest led into captivity; and, scattered through the, world, they continue without king, or temple, or true worship, to the present day. "But do not these last verses contain a promise that all the nations of the earth shall be brought under the dominion of the Church of Christ; that all heathen and ungodly kings shall be put down, and pious men put in their places?" I do not think so. I believe God never intended that his Church should have the civil government of the world. His Church like its Founder and Head, will never be a ruler and divider among men. The men who under pretense of superior sanctity, affect this, are not of God; the truth of God is not in them; they are puffed up with pride, and fall into the condemnation of the devil. Wo unto the inhabitants of the earth, when the Church takes the civil government of the world into its hand! Were it possible that God should trust religious people with civil government, anarchy would soon ensue; for every professed believer in Christ would consider himself on a par with any other and every other believer, the right to rule and the necessity to obey would be immediately lost, and every man would do what was right in his own eyes; for, where the grace of God makes all equal, who can presume to say, I have Divine authority to govern my fellow? The Church of Rome has claimed this right; and the pope, in consequence, became a secular prince; but the nations of the world have seen the vanity and iniquity of the claim, and refused allegiance. Those whom it did govern, with force and with cruelty did it rule them; and the odious yoke is now universally cast off. Certain enthusiasts and hypocrites, not of that Church, have also attempted to set up a fifth monarchy, a civil government by the Saints! and diabolic saints they were. To such pretenders God gives neither countenance nor support. The secular and spiritual government God will ever keep distinct; and the Church shall have no power but that of doing good; and this only in proportion to its holiness, heavenly-mindedness, and piety to God. That the verses above may be understood in a spiritual sense, as applicable to the influence of the word of God preached, may be seen in the following analysis.  <chapter eID="Ps.149"/> <div eID="gen23632" type="x-p"/>

entries.c555539a9f8d0b8b6634e6281bdb7b7cae754671: <reference osisRef="Ps.149.1-Ps.149.5">Psa 149:1-5</reference> <div eID="gen10348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10349" type="x-p"/> A period, in which the church is renewing its youth and drawing nearer to the form it is finally to assume, also of inward necessity puts forth new songs. Such a new era has now dawned for the church of the saints, the Israel that has remained faithful to its God and the faith of its fathers. The Creator of Israel (עשׂיו, plural, with the plural suffix, like עשׂי in <reference osisRef="Job.35.10">Job 35:10</reference>, עשׂיך in <reference osisRef="Isa.54.5">Isa 54:5</reference>, cf. עשׂו in <reference osisRef="Job.40.19">Job 40:19</reference>; according to Hupfeld and Hitzig, cf. Ew. §256, <hi type="italic">b</hi>, Ges. §93, 9, singular; but <hi type="italic">aj , ajich , aw</hi>, are always really plural suffixes) has shown that He is also Israel’s Preserver and the King of Zion, that He cannot leave the children of Zion for any length of time under foreign dominion, and has heard the sighing of the exiles (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.19">Isa 63:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.13">Isa 26:13</reference>). Therefore the church newly appropriated by its God and King is to celebrate Him, whose Name shines forth anew out of its history, with festive dance, timbrel, and cithern. For (as the occasion, hitherto only hinted at, is now expressly stated) Jahve takes a pleasure in His people; His wrath in comparison with His mercy is only like a swiftly passing moment (Isa 54:7.). The futures that follow state that which is going on at the present time. ענוים is, as frequently, a designation of the <hi type="italic">ecclesia pressa</hi>, which has hitherto, amidst patient endurance of suffering, waited for God’s own act of redemption. He now adorns them with ישׁוּעה, help against the victory over the hostile world; now the saints, hitherto enslaved and contemned, exult בכבוד, in honour, or on account of the honour which vindicates them before the world and is anew bestowed upon them (בּ of the reason, or, which is more probable in connection with the boldness of the expression, of the state and mood);<note placement="foot">Such, too (with pomp, not “with an army”), is the meaning of μετὰ δόξης in 1 Macc. 10:60; 14:4, 5, vid., Grimm <hi type="italic">in loc.</hi>)</note> they shout for joy upon their beds, upon which they have hitherto poured forth their complaints over the present (cf. Hos 7:14), and ardently longed for a better future (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.8">Isa 26:8</reference>); for the bed is the place of soliloquy (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.5">Psa 4:5</reference>), and the tears shed there (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.7">Psa 6:7</reference>) are turned into shouts of joy in the case of Israel.
entries.404f043a5802e2adcd8455f4b3e8bcde4d2d4d95: <reference osisRef="Ps.149.6-Ps.149.9">Psa 149:6-9</reference> <div eID="gen10349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10350" type="x-p"/> The glance is here directed to the future. The people of the present have again, in their God, attained to a lofty self-consciousness, the consciousness of their destiny, viz., to subjugate the whole world of nations to the God of Israel. In the presence of the re-exaltation which they have experienced their throat is full of words and songs exalting Jahve (רוממות, plural of רומם, or, according to another reading, רומם, Psa 56:1-13 :17), and as servants of this God, the rightful Lord of all the heathen (<reference osisRef="Ps.82.8">Psa 82:8</reference>), they hold in their hand a many-mouthed, i.e., many edged sword (vid., <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, p. 580), in order to take the field on behalf of the true religion, as the Maccabees actually did, not long after: ταῖς μὲν χερσὶν ἀγωνιζόμενοι ταῖς δὲ καρδίαις πρὸς τὸν Θεόν εὐχόμενοι (2 Macc. 15:27). The meaning of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.149.9">Psa 149:9</reference></hi> becomes a different one, according as we take this line as co-ordinate or subordinate to what goes before. Subordinated, it would imply the execution of a penal jurisdiction over those whom they carried away, and כּתוּב would refer to prescriptive facts such as are recorded in Num 31:8; 1Sa 15:32. (Hitzig). But it would become the religious lyric poet least of all to entertain such an unconditional prospect of the execution of the conquered worldly rulers. There is just as little ground for thinking of the judgment of extermination pronounced upon the nations of Canaan, which was pronounced upon them for an especial reason. If <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.149.9">Psa 149:9</reference></hi> is taken as co-ordinate, the “written judgment” (<hi type="italic">Recht</hi>) consists in the complete carrying out of the subjugation; and this is commended by the perfectly valid parallel, Isa 45:14. The poet, however, in connection with the expression “written,” has neither this nor that passage of Scripture in his mind, but the testimony of the Law and of prophecy in general, that all kingdoms shall become God’s and His Christ's. Subjugation (and certainly not without bloodshed) is the scriptural משׁפּט for the execution of which Jahve makes use of His own nation. Because the God who thus vindicates Himself is Israel’s God, this subjugation of the world is הדר, splendour and glory, to all who are in love devoted to Him. The glorifying of Jahve is also the glorifying of Israel.  <chapter eID="Ps.149"/> <div eID="gen10350" type="x-p"/>

entries.70f833c12dc56e3b651381e501d653e315e1052a:
PSALM 149
If we may be allowed to compare this Psalm with the former ones, and the next, which is the last, the only difference is, that while the author of the Psalm, whoever he was, has hitherto spoken of God’s special care and protection of his Church in connection with the common providential government of the world, here he speaks of his benefits to the Church exclusively. In the next Psalm mention is only made of the power of God in general.
Hallelujah.
Psalm 149:1-4
1. Sing ye to Jehovah a new song: his praise is in the congregation of the merciful. 2. Let Israel rejoice in his Maker: let the sons of Zion rejoice their king.
“The Jewish government was a Theocracy, which commenced at the time of the departure from Egypt; and continued in some degree till the coming of Christ, as had been foretold by Jacob, Genesis 49:10.” — Dimock.
3. Let them praise his name on the pipe,
In our English Bible it is in the text, “in the dance;” and on the margin, “or with the pipe.” מחול machol, the Hebrew word employed, is often in our authorized version rendered “dance”; but this is not its meaning. It denotes, as Parkhurst states, “some fistular wind instrument of music, with holes, as a flute, pipe or fife, from חל, chal to make a hole or opening.” “I know no place in the Bible.” Says Dr. Adam Clark, “where מחול, mechol, and מחלת, mechalath, mean dance of any kind; they constantly mean some kind of pipe.”
on the timbrel
The Hebrew name for this kind of this musical instrument is תף, toph. The timbrel, tympanum, or tambourine, was used chiefly by women, and was employed in choral dances, or occasions of religious or festal processions. Thus we read in Exodus 15:20, 21, “And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and dances. And Miriam answered them, Sing ye to the Lord, for he hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea.” The principle of the פף, toph, or timbrel was that of a prepared skin stretched upon a hoop or frame. There were various kinds or forms of this instrument. “Our common tambourine, with small cymbals inserted in the frame, also appears in some paintings, [of Egyptian and European antiquity,] and is now very common in Western Asia. We are told that the frame was either of metal or wood and that the ass’s skin was usually employed for the covering. They were not always played by the naked hand; but were sometimes struck with small batons, or with a knotty whip with many thongs, instead of which, on particular festivals, a sprig of some tree or plant, considered suitable to the occasion, was sometimes employed.” — Illustrated Commentary upon the Bible. The timbrel is evidently of oriental origin. From the reference to it in Genesis 31:27, where תף is translated “tabret,” we learn that it was known in the time of Jacob, that is, ages previous to the existence of the great European nations of antiquity; and both the Greeks and Romans confessed that their instruments of this class were derived from Egyptians and Syrians. See volume 3
and the harp let them sing psalms to him. 4. Because Jehovah hath taken pleasure in his people; he will glorify the poor unto salvation.
 
1. Sing to Jehovah a new song. This exordium proves what I have just said, that the exhortation now given is addressed only to God’s people; for the singular goodness which is particularly extended to them affords more ample matter of praise. The probable conjecture is, that the Psalm was composed at the time when the people were begun to rejoice, or after they had returned to their native country from the Babylonish captivity. We will see from the context that a promise is given of recovery from their ruined condition. The object, I think, of the Psalmist, is to encourage them to expect the full and complete deliverance, some prelude of which had been suddenly and unexpectedly given in the permission to return. As the Church was not fully restored at once, but was with difficulty and only after a long period brought to a state of vigor, comfort such as this was much needed. The Spirit of God would also furnish a remedy for evils which were afterwards to break out; for the Church had scarcely begun to respire when it was again harassed with various evils, and oppressed by the cruel tyranny of Antiochus, which was followed up by a dreadful dispersion. The Psalmist had good reason therefore for animating the godly to look forward for the full accomplishment of the mercy of God, that they might be persuaded of divine protection until such time as the Messiah should arise who would gather all Israel. He calls this a new song, as we have noticed elsewhere, to distinguish it from those with which the saints commonly and daily praised God, for praise is their continued exercise. It follows that he speaks of some rare and unusual benefit, demanding signal and particular thanksgiving. And I am disposed to think that whoever may have been the author of the Psalm, he alludes to that passage in Isaiah, (Isaiah 42:10,) “Sing unto the Lord a new song,” when he speaks of the future restoration of the Church, and the eternal kingdom of Christ. In the second clause of the verse there is a promise implied. For though he proceeds to exhort the Lord’s people to sing God’s praises together, he hints along with this that the Church would coalesce again into one body, so as to celebrate God’s praises in the solemn assembly. We know that so scattered were the Israelites, that the sacred songs ceased to be sung, as elsewhere they complain of being called upon to sing —
“How shall we sing the songs of the Lord in a strange land?” (Psalm 137:4.)
He bids them prepare therefore after this sad dispersion for holding their sacred assemblies again.

                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CXLIX.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>The scope and design of this Psalm is to stir up and encou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rage Gods people to praise him, either 1. for their deli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verance out of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> and the promises which God had given them of the perfection of that work and of the en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />largement of their power and dominion in the world: or rather, 2. for the establishment of the Kingdom of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> hands, and for that safety and glory and victory over their enemies which they expected by that means. But withal, the Psalmist, or the Spirit of God which dicta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted this Psalm to him, had a further prospect, even to the Messiah, of whom <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> was a Type, and who was to succeed <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> in the Throne, and to bring that Kingdom to its highest perfection. And so divers of the Jewish Doctors understand this Psalm.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> Hallelu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jah.</ns0:note> PRaise ye the LORD. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 33. 3.</ns0:note> Sing unto the LORD a new song <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">For these new mercies conferred upon us, denied to former times.</ns0:note>: <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> his praise in the congregation of saints.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Let Israel rejoyce in <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 100. 3.</ns0:note> him that made him <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">That made them not onely his creatures, but, which is unspeakably greater, his people: or, that advanced and adorned them with singular priviledges, as this word is used, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 12. 6. and elsewhere.</ns0:note>: let the children of Zion be joyful in their king <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> and his posterity, and especially the chief of all of them, the Messiah. Let them rejoyce and bless God that they have so potent, so wise, and so just a King.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 81. 2.</ns0:note> Let them praise his Name <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> with the pipe.</ns0:note> in the dance: let them sing <ns0:hi>praises</ns0:hi> unto him with the timbrel and harp <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">According to the usage of that time and dispensation.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 For the LORD taketh pleasure in his peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">He loveth them above all people, and rejoyceth over them to do them good.</ns0:note>: he will beautifie <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>adorn</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>glorifie,</ns0:hi> make them amiable and honourable in the eyes of the world, who now hate and despise them.</ns0:note> the meek <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>humble,</ns0:hi> to wit, his people, as he now said, who are oft in Scripture described by that character, because all true Israelites are such, and all Israe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lites profess and ought to be such. Or, <ns0:hi>the afflicted,</ns0:hi> as that word is oft used in Scripture, which hath been observed before, his poor afflicted and oppressed people, to whom the following salvation is most needful and acceptable.</ns0:note> with salva<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Both temporal, in delivering them from, and setting them above, all their enemies, and afterwards, with everlasting salvation and glory.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Let the saints be joyful in glory <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">For the honour which God putteth upon them.</ns0:note>: let them sing aloud upon their beds <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, 1. for their safe and sweet repose and peace, which is signified by <ns0:hi>resting in beds, Isa.</ns0:hi> 57. 2. or, 2. by night as well as by day, even in the time devoted to rest and sleep, which they shall borrow to praise God for his eminent and extraor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinary blessings, as <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> frequently did upon such occasions.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 <ns0:hi>Let</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />altations.</ns0:note> the high praises of God <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> in their throat.</ns0:note> in their mouth <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>in their throat.</ns0:hi> Which signifies vocal praise, and that with a loud voice.</ns0:note>, and a <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Heb. 4. 12. Rev. 1. 16.</ns0:note> two-edged sword in their hand <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Not onely to defend themselves from their enemies, but, as it follows, to revenge themselves upon them.</ns0:note>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 To execute vengeance upon the heathen <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">For all their cruelties and injuries towards Gods people. This was literally accomplished by <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> upon the Philistines, Ammonites, Syrians, and other neighbouring Nations and Princes, which were bitter enemies to Gods people. And the same thing was done afterward in the Christian world, when God raised up Christian Princes, who did by the help of the Christians fighting with and under them, severely re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venge the blood of the martyred Christians upon their cruel Persecutors and Tyrants in divers ages. It may also be un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood of the spiritual plagues which Christ by the hand or ministry of his Apostles and Ministers did inflict upon the hearts and consciences of his incorrigible enemies, who by Gods word and ordinances were either tormented or hard<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned to their destruction. Yea it may have a respect unto the last day of judgment, in which the Saints shall judge the world, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 6. 2. which will be a most dreadful execution of this vengeance, &c.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> punishments upon the people.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 To bind their kings with chains, and their nobles with fetters of iron <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Of which see the Note on the foregoing verse.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 7. 1, 2.</ns0:note> To execute upon them the judgment written <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Appointed and declared in the holy Scripture, as <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 12. 32. & 29. 19. & 32. 41, 42, 43. and elsewhere. This is added to shew that they do not this work to satisfie their own malicious or revengeful inclinations, but in obedience to Gods commands, and onely in such manner as God hath allowed in his word.</ns0:note>: this honour have all his saints <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The honour of these actions belongs to all the Saints, for whose sakes God appointed this in his word, and afterwards executed it by his providence.</ns0:note>. Praise ye the LORD.</ns0:p>
